danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Syv år var gået. Det stormfulde hav af europæisk historie havde trukket sig tilbage inden for sine kyster og syntes at være faldet til ro. Men de mystiske kræfter, der bevæger menneskeheden (mystiske, fordi lovene for deres bevægelse er ukendte for os), fortsatte med at virke.

Selv om havets overflade af historie syntes ubevægeligt, fortsatte menneskehedens bevægelse lige så uophørligt som tidens strøm. Forskellige grupper af mennesker dannedes og opløstes; den kommende dannelse og opløsning af riger og folkevandringer var under forberedelse.

Historiens hav blev ikke længere kastet spasmodisk fra kyst til kyst som tidligere. Det sydede i sine dybder. De historiske skikkelser blev ikke længere båret af bølgerne fra den ene kyst til den anden som før. De syntes nu at rotere på ét sted. De historiske skikkelser i spidsen for hære, der førhen havde afspejlet folkemassernes bevægelse ved at beordre krige, felttog og slag, afspejlede nu den boblende strøm ved politiske og diplomatiske kampe, love og traktater.
Historikerne kalder de historiske skikkelsers aktivitet i denne periode for »reaktionen«.

I deres behandling af denne periode fordømmer de strengt de historiske personer, der efter deres mening forårsagede det, de beskriver som reaktionen. Alle den tids kendte personligheder, fra Aleksandr og Napoleon til Madame de Staël, Photius, Schelling, Fichte, Chateaubriand og resten, stilles for denne strenge domstol og frikendes eller fordømmes alt efter, om de fremmede fremskridtet eller reaktionen.

Ifølge deres beretninger fandt der også en reaktion sted i Rusland på dette tidspunkt, og hovedsynderen var Aleksandr den Første — den samme mand, der ifølge dem var hovedårsagen til den liberale bevægelse ved begyndelsen af sin regeringstid og var Ruslands frelser.
Der er ingen i russisk litteratur nu, fra skoleeleven til den lærde historiker, der ikke kaster sin lille sten efter Aleksandr for ting, han gjorde forkert i denne periode af sin regeringstid.

»Han burde have handlet på denne måde og på den måde. I dette tilfælde gjorde han det godt, og i det tilfælde dårligt. Han opførte sig beundringsværdigt i begyndelsen af sin regeringstid og under 1812, men handlede forkert ved at give Polen en forfatning, danne Den Hellige Alliance, overlade magten til Araktjejev, begunstige Golitsyn og mystikerne, og senere Sjiskov og Fotius. Han handlede forkert ved at bekymre sig om hærens frontlinje og ved at afskedige regimenter; han handlede forkert ved at bruge sin magt på denne og hin måde.«
Det ville kræve et dusin sider at opregne alle de bebrejdelser, historikerne retter mod ham, baseret på deres viden om, hvad der er godt for menneskeheden.
Hvad betyder disse bebrejdelser?

Udspringer de selvsamme handlinger, som historikerne roser Aleksandr den Første for (de liberale tiltag i begyndelsen af hans regeringstid, hans kamp mod Napoleon, den fasthed han udviste i 1812 og felttoget i 1813) — udspringer de ikke af de selvsamme kilder: hans fødsel, opdragelse og livs omstændigheder — der gjorde hans person til det, den var, og hvorfra også de handlinger flød, som historikerne bebrejder ham?
Hvori ligger substansen af disse bebrejdelser?

Den ligger i det faktum, at en historisk skikkelse som Aleksandr den Første, stående på det højest mulige tinde af menneskelig magt med historiens blændende lys rettet mod sig — en skikkelse udsat for de stærkeste af alle indflydelser: de intriger, det smigreri og det selvbedrag, der er uadskillelige fra magten — en skikkelse, der på hvert øjeblik af sit liv følte et ansvar for alt, hvad der skete i Europa — og ikke en opdigtet person, men et levende væsen med alle sine personlige vaner, lidenskaber og stræben efter det gode, det skønne og det sande — at denne skikkelse for halvtreds år siden ikke kun ikke var dydig (det bebrejder historikerne ham ikke), men ikke havde de synspunkter på, hvad der er godt for menneskeheden, som en nutidig professor har, der fra ungdommen har beskæftiget sig med lærdom, det vil sige med at læse bøger og høre forelæsninger og tage noter fra disse bøger og forelæsninger.

Men selv om vi antager, at Aleksandr den Første for halvtreds år siden tog fejl i sit syn på, hvad der var godt for folket, må vi uundgåeligt antage, at den historiker, der dømmer Aleksandr, også efter nogen tid vil vise sig at have taget fejl i sit syn på, hvad der er godt for menneskeheden. Den antagelse ligger så meget nærmere, som vi kan se, at med hvert år og med hver ny forfatter skifter meningen om, hvad der er godt for menneskeheden. Det, der engang så godt ud, tager sig ti år senere dårligt ud, og omvendt. Ja, selv på én og samme tid møder man stik modsatte meninger om godt og ondt i historien. Nogle roser Aleksandr for at have givet Polen en forfatning og stiftet Den Hellige Alliance, andre dadler ham for de samme handlinger.

De historiske personers aktivitet — Aleksandr eller Napoleons — kan ikke kaldes nyttig eller skadelig, for det er umuligt at sige, hvad den var nyttig eller skadelig for. Hvis den aktivitet mishager nogen, er det kun, fordi den ikke stemmer overens med hans begrænsede forståelse af, hvad der er godt. Hvad enten bevarelsen af min fars hus i Moskva i 1812, eller det russiske hærs ære, eller Petersborg eller andre universiteter trivsel, eller Polens frihed, eller Ruslands storhed, eller magtbalancen i Europa, eller en bestemt form for europæisk civilisation kaldet fremskridt, forekommer mig godt — må jeg indrømme, at enhver historisk persons aktivitet foruden disse formål også tjente andre, mere almene formål, som er utilgængelige for mig.

Men lad os antage, at det, der kaldes videnskab, kan forene alle modsætninger og besidder en uforanderlig målestok for godt og ondt, hvormed historiske personer og begivenheder kan bedømmes; lad os sige, at Aleksandr kunne have gjort alt anderledes; lad os sige, at han med vejledning fra dem, der bebrejder ham, og som lader som om de kender menneskehedens endelige mål, kunne have fulgt det program for nationalitet, frihed, lighed og fremskridt (der synes at være det nuværende programs mål), som hans nutidige kritikere ville have foreskrevet ham. Lad os antage, at dette program var muligt og allerede formuleret, og at Aleksandr havde handlet i overensstemmelse med det. Hvad ville der så være blevet af alle de andres aktivitet, der modsatte sig datidens regeringsretning — en aktivitet, som efter kritikernes mening var god og gavnlig? Deres aktivitet ville ikke have eksisteret; der ville intet liv have været; der ville intet have været overhovedet.
Hvis vi indrømmer, at menneskelivet kan styres af fornuften, ødelægges muligheden for liv.

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Seven years had passed. The storm-tossed sea of European history had subsided within its shores and seemed to have grown calm. But the mysterious forces that move humanity—mysterious because the laws governing them are unknown to us—continued to operate.

Though the surface of the sea of history appeared motionless, the movement of humanity went on as ceaselessly as the flow of time. Various groups of people formed and dissolved, the formation and dissolution of kingdoms and displacements of peoples were in preparation.

The sea of history was no longer driven violently from shore to shore as before. It was churning in its depths. Historical figures were no longer carried by the waves from one shore to another. They now seemed to spin in place. Historical figures who had formerly commanded armies and directed the movement of masses through wars, campaigns, and battles now guided the surging masses through political and diplomatic maneuvers, laws, and treaties.
Historians call this activity of historical figures "the reaction."

In describing this period, they sternly condemn the historical figures who, in their view, caused what they call the reaction. All the prominent people of that era—from Alexander and Napoleon to Madame de Stael, Photius, Schelling, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others—are arraigned before their stern tribunal and acquitted or condemned according to whether they promoted progress or reaction.

According to these accounts, a reaction took place in Russia too at this time, and the chief culprit was Alexander I—the same man who, according to these same historians, was the chief cause of the liberal reforms at the start of his reign, the savior of Russia, and the hero of Europe. Yet in present-day Russian literature, from schoolboy essayists to serious historians, there is no one who does not criticize Alexander for the things he supposedly did wrong during this period.
There is no one in Russian literature now, from schoolboy essayists to learned historians, who does not take a shot at Alexander for his mistakes during this phase of his reign.

"He should have acted this way, not that way. In this case he did well; in that case, badly. He was admirable at the start of his reign and during 1812, but was wrong to give a constitution to Poland, create the Holy Alliance, empower Arakcheyev, encourage Golitsyn and mysticism, and then encourage Shishkov and Photius. He was wrong to interfere with the army's front-line administration; he was wrong to disband the Semyonovsky regiment, and so on and so on."
It would take a dozen pages to list all the criticisms historians make of him, based on their knowledge of what is good for humanity.
What do these criticisms mean?

Don't the very actions for which historians praise Alexander I—the liberal reforms at the start of his reign, the struggle with Napoleon, the firmness he showed in 1812, and the campaign of 1813—flow from the same sources, the same conditions of birth, education, and life that shaped Alexander's personality and produced the actions for which historians blame him, such as the Holy Alliance, the restoration of Poland, and the reaction of the 1820s?
What is the real substance of these criticisms?

It amounts to this. Here was a man at the very summit of human power, with the blinding light of history on him. Exposed to all the intrigue, flattery and self-deception that go with such power, he felt at every instant responsible for everything that happened in Europe. Nor was Alexander I a fictional character: he was alive, with his own habits and passions and, like anyone, his own impulses toward goodness, beauty and truth. The historians do not charge him with a lack of virtue. Their charge is that fifty years ago he did not hold the same view of human welfare as a professor today who has spent his life since boyhood on scholarship, that is, on books, lectures, and notes taken from them.

But even if we assume that Alexander was mistaken fifty years ago in his idea of what was good for the people, we must also assume that the historian who judges him will, after some time, also turn out to be wrong in his understanding of what is good for humanity. This assumption is all the more natural and inevitable because the development of history shows us that every year, with every new writer, what we consider good for humanity changes. What once seemed good looks bad ten years later, and vice versa. In fact, even at the same moment people hold entirely contradictory views of good and bad in history. Some praise Alexander for giving Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance. Others condemn him for those very acts.

Alexander's activity, or Napoleon's, cannot be called useful or harmful, because we cannot say what it was useful or harmful for. If someone dislikes it, that is only because it doesn't match their limited understanding of what is good. Whether I see the preservation of my father's house in Moscow in 1812 as good, or the glory of the Russian army, or the prosperity of Petersburg's university or Poland's freedom, or Russia's greatness, or Europe's balance of power, or a certain kind of European civilization called "progress"—I must acknowledge that the activity of any historical figure had, besides these aims, other aims more broadly and universally human that are beyond my grasp.

But let us suppose that what is called science can reconcile all contradictions and possesses an unchanging standard of good and bad by which to judge historical characters and events; let us say that Alexander could have done everything differently; let us even say that—guided by those who criticize him, who claim to know the ultimate goal of humanity's movement—he could have followed the program of nationalism, freedom, equality, and progress (for there seems to be no other) that his present-day critics would prescribe for him. Let us assume all that was possible. What then would have become of the activity of all the people who opposed the direction that the government was taking at that time? Their activity would not have existed; there would have been no life; there would have been nothing.
If we accept that human life can be governed by reason, then the very possibility of life is destroyed.
